walkthroughs.title: EQT, August 2011: a leader flush in a fear spike
steps: EQT, August 2011. A leader up 32% falls five straight days, 25.2% in all, in a market sell-off.

walkthroughs.title: ACMR, September 2020: the post-blow-off snapback
steps: ACMR, September 2020. A stock up 79% runs parabolic, then breaks. Three down days, 38.6% lost, 39% under its 10-session high.
The flush: 3.5 ATR on 3.5x volume, the heaviest of the chart. RSI(2) at 0. Five stretch marks. We wait.

questions.q: In one line, what is a mean-reversion long?
choices: A bounce after a short, fast drop
A breakout of a quiet, flat base
A hold for months in a leader
Buying any stock down a lot
questions.answer: A bounce after a short, fast drop
questions.why: A bounce after a short, fast drop. Our card defines it as a swing trade against a short, unusually fast move, aimed at a return to a short average. Stockbee: extreme strength or weakness tends to mean revert in short time frames. It is not a breakout and not a long hold. Nor is it any falling stock: the leader flush needs a leader above its 200-day and 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: We trade the snapback after an unusually fast drop.

wrong.A breakout of a quiet, flat base: That is a base breakout. Mean reversion buys after a drop, not after quiet.
wrong.A hold for months in a leader: That is a trend hold. This is a swing trade aimed at a short average, so the hold is short.
wrong.Buying any stock down a lot: A big fall is not enough. The leader flush needs a leader above its 200-day and 50-day, up at least 25% first.

questions.simple: It is a short bounce trade after a stock drops unusually fast, aimed at a snap back toward a short average.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-016, the definition and hold length)

questions.q: We buy a leader flush only when the stock sat above its 50-day and 200-day before the drop.
questions.why: True. For the leader flush, the stock sits above its 200-day and its 50-day the day before the flush. It is also up at least 25% in the prior 1 to 3 months. Our 200-day rule bars longs below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic long, which is a different setup. StockCharts also looks for buys above the 200-day and shorts below it.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the dip in strength. A stock under its 200-day is not our dip.
questions.simple: True, because we buy this flush only in a strong stock that was above its 50-day and 200-day lines before the drop.

So under 10 is a dip, and under 5 is the deep stretch the mark asks for. A mark measures the stretch. It is not the buy signal: we still wait for the turn.

questions.simple: 5, because StockCharts reports Connors did better buying a 2-period RSI dip under 5 than one under 10.

Bonde adds that the 2RSI entry is meaningless if there is no trend. So the mark only measures the stretch. The trend check and the turn decide the trade.

StockCharts warns that the RSI(2) signal can be early, because moves often continue after it. Buying the close of the flush day buys a price that may still be falling.
questions.lesson_line: A falling price is not a trigger. The turn is.

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a mean-reversion long?
choices: Just under the flush day's low
Under the rising 50-day line
A fixed 5% under your entry
Right at the flush day's low
questions.answer: Just under the flush day's low
questions.why: Just under the flush day's low. The stop goes a few cents under the flush low, or under the turn day's low if that is lower. It sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. The stop comes first and the size comes from it. Kell also puts his stop just below the low of the reversal bar.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the flush low.

wrong.A fixed 5% under your entry: A fixed percent ignores the chart. The stop comes first, from the flush low, and the size comes from the stop.
wrong.Right at the flush day's low: Our rule puts the stop a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
wrong.Under the rising 50-day line: The stop comes from the flush low, not from an average. It goes a few cents under the flush low, or the turn day's low if that is lower.

questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the flush day's low, not right on it.

questions.q: Mean-reversion flush or something else?

A mean-reversion flush day
A gap-down oops reversal
An undercut and rally

Six quiet sessions to the rising 20 EMA, never more than 1 ATR a day, is that drift. A flush is a hard, fast stretch, such as a 2 ATR day. The flush card skips a slow, controlled decline as not stretched enough.
questions.lesson_line: A drift is a pullback. A flush is a shock.

wrong.A mean-reversion flush day: A flush is a hard, fast day. This is a slow drift with no big day.
wrong.A gap-down oops reversal: An oops gaps under the prior day's low and reclaims the prior close the same day. Nothing like that happened here.
wrong.An undercut and rally: An undercut and rally undercuts a visible level after an ordinary dip. This drift undercut nothing.

questions.story: A leader drifts for six sessions on light volume to its rising 20 EMA. No day drops more than 1 ATR.

deeper.trap: A pullback to a rising 20-day looks like a dip to buy. The card even lists the rising 20 or 50-day as a level. But a level is only half of this setup. It also needs a real stretch with range or volume expansion. A slow, controlled decline is not one.

Mean-reversion flush
Moving-average pullback
Undercut and rally

wrong.Moving-average pullback: A pullback drifts on light volume. Four gaps and a 45% fall is no drift.
wrong.Undercut and rally: An undercut and rally dips under a visible level after an ordinary dip, with no volume needed. Four straight gap downs are no ordinary dip.

questions.story: A stock gaps down four days in a row. It ends 45% off its peak.
questions.simple: It is a parabolic long, because four straight gap downs make a multi-day burst, not a one-day flush.

questions.q: Which setup is this?

A mean-reversion flush
A parabolic long setup
An oops reversal day

A 3% dip under clear support on ordinary volume, closed back above it the same day, fits. A flush is a hard, fast drop with range or volume expansion. A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gap downs. An oops needs a gap.

wrong.A parabolic long setup: A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gap downs. This is one ordinary dip.
wrong.An oops reversal day: An oops gaps under the prior day's low in an orderly pullback. This dip under a level had no gap.

questions.story: A leader dips 3% under a clear support level on ordinary volume, with no gap. It closes back above the level the same day.
questions.simple: It is an undercut and rally, because an ordinary dip broke a clear level for a moment and got back above it.

deeper.trap: An undercut that reclaims a level the same day looks like a flush that turned. The difference is the drop before it. An undercut and rally follows an ordinary dip and needs no volume. A flush needs a real stretch with range or volume expansion, not a slow, controlled decline.

questions.q: Flush or something else?
choices: An oops reversal
A mean-reversion flush
A moving-average pullback
A parabolic long
questions.why: An oops reversal. That card's setup gaps under the prior day's low in an orderly pullback 3% to 12% off the high. It reclaims the prior close the same day. A calm pullback 6% off the high fits. A flush is a hard, stretched drop, not a calm pullback. A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gap downs, not one gap.
questions.lesson_line: Orderly pullback, gap under, reclaim the same day: oops.

wrong.A mean-reversion flush: A flush is a hard, fast drop, not a calm pullback.
wrong.A moving-average pullback: A moving-average pullback drifts on light volume to a rising line. This one gapped under the prior day's low and reclaimed the prior close.
wrong.A parabolic long: A parabolic long is a multi-day burst of gap downs. This is one gap in a calm pullback.

questions.story: A leader is 6% off its high after a calm pullback. It gaps under the prior day's low, then reclaims the prior close the same day.
questions.simple: It is an oops reversal, because it gapped under the prior day's low and won back the prior close that day.

deeper.trap: The oops and the flush both turn up after a drop, so the turn alone does not name the setup. Look at what came before. An oops follows an orderly pullback 3% to 12% off the high. A flush follows a hard stretch, such as a 2 ATR day or 3 or more straight down closes. Name the setup first, then use its rules.

questions.q: Why do we pass?

It is above the 200-day
The flush is too big
Four days is too few

It is a stock rolling over from a top, not a leader stretched down. Sitting above the averages fits, and a 2.1 ATR flush fits. Four down days is plenty. The missing piece is the run.
questions.lesson_line: No leader's run, no leader flush.

wrong.It is above the 200-day: Being above the 200-day is what the setup wants.
wrong.The flush is too big: A 2.1 ATR flush is what a flush looks like. The run before it is what is missing.
wrong.Four days is too few: Four down days is plenty. The card skips only the first or second down day.

questions.story: A stock is up 15% from its 63-day low. It slides four days, a 2.1 ATR flush, and still sits above both averages.
questions.simple: We pass because it was only up 15%, and a leader flush needs a run of at least 25% first.

deeper.trap: A stock above both averages with a hard flush looks like the setup. The trap is skipping the first check: was it a leader? Measure the run from the 63-day low before the slide. Up 15% is a stock rolling over from a top. The card's form A starts at 25%.

questions.q: The turn prints the next morning. How do you read it?

Too small a run to be a leader
A moving-average pullback to buy
A stretched leader, ripe to bounce

wrong.A moving-average pullback to buy: A moving-average pullback drifts on light volume to a rising line. This slid through the 50-day into a 3x volume flush.
wrong.A stretched leader, ripe to bounce: Eight days through the 50-day after a parabolic top is a broken leader, not a stretched one. RSI(2) at 0 does not fix that.
wrong.Too small a run to be a leader: Form A wants a run of at least 25%, and this one was up 58%. The run was fine. The trend broke.

questions.story: A stock just made a parabolic top, up 58%. It falls seven straight days, closing under its 50-day. Day eight is a 3x volume flush, 21% down in all, with RSI(2) at 0.
questions.simple: It was a broken trend, because eight down days through the 50-day after a parabolic top is a break, not a stretch.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the marks alone. Eight straight down days, a 3x volume flush and RSI(2) at 0 all shout oversold. But the slide went through the 50-day right after a parabolic top. That is a broken leader, not a stretched one. Check the trend before you count marks.

Buy back at once, since it is cheaper
Widen the next stop to give it room
Write the stock off for good
